claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among the alloys arise from changes in local chemical ordering and lattice distortion rather than constituent count alone.
Adding a fifth constituent to form equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni perturbs local chemical ordering relative to the quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quinary alloy has greater lattice distortion than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
Changes in local chemical ordering and lattice distortion modify the stacking-fault-energy distribution.
The modified stacking-fault-energy distribution changes dislocation interactions.
Changes in stacking-fault energy and dislocation interactions alter the balance between dislocation slip and deformation twinning.
The balance between slip and twinning governs strain hardening and failure behavior.
The fifth constituent lowers the barrier for homogeneous dislocation nucleation.
The proposed changes in dislocation nucleation, stacking-fault energy, slip, and twinning increase strain hardening and delay plastic instability.
Under identical testing conditions, the quinary alloy will have a higher strain-hardening rate than its quaternary and ternary counterparts.
Under identical testing conditions, the quinary alloy will show a later onset of plastic instability than its quaternary and ternary counterparts.
The comparison is restricted to equiatomic, single-phase FCC alloys with similar microstructures produced by identical thermomechanical processing.
The proposed mechanism is intended to apply at ambient temperature and moderate, fixed strain rates.
The proposed relationship may not hold when grain-size effects or high-temperature phenomena dominate.
Identical standardized processing can ensure identical grain size and defect density across the quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys.
Atom-probe tomography or an analogous technique can quantitatively assess the relevant short-range order and stacking-fault-energy differences.
